082:1: How did the instinct to mate grow, through the rules of society, into the home, the chief institution of civilization?
082:4: In Paper 81 we looked at the tools, institutions, and factors that uphold civilization, and we saw that among them the home is the basic institution that passes on the torch of culture. Now Paper 82 traces the roots of that home: how marriage arose and grew.
082:5: Marriage is man's reactional adjustment to the two sexes, and family life is the sum of all such adjustments. Because marriage is the basis of all social evolution, it is certain to continue in some form, and it has given mankind the home (82:0.1). Religious, social, and educational institutions are needed too, but a child learns most of what life requires in the home and the neighborhood. That is why the home, as an educational institution, must be preserved (82:0.2-0.3).
082:6: How, then, did primitive mating, almost without any regulation, become today's marriage by way of taboos, mores, and ideas of property? And what does that long process teach us?
082:8: ⟦Q 82:0.1⟧Marriage has given mankind the home, and the home is the crowning glory of the whole long and arduous evolutionary struggle.⟦/Q⟧ (82:0.1)
082:12: However great the personality differences between man and woman, the sex urge is enough to bring the two together for the reproduction of the species. This instinct was at work long before people knew anything of love, devotion, or marital loyalty. Mating is an innate tendency, and marriage is its social repercussion (82:1.1). For primitive man sex was not a dominating passion, and the book explains that strong sex passion arose chiefly as the imagination and aesthetic sense of the Andite inheritance were blended in (82:1.2).
082:14: What the regulation of sex in marriage indicates
082:17: The demand that the sex urge be channeled into useful paths according to the mores
082:19: Sex reveals both the highest and the lowest
082:21: The mating instinct is the one emotion that leads selfish human beings to put the welfare and perpetuation of the species far above their personal comfort (82:1.7). When food becomes plentiful, the sex urge easily comes to the fore, and since human desire is not periodic as it is in animals, society must demand self-control (82:1.9). Secrecy and hypocrisy only hide the problem; they do not solve it (82:1.10).
082:23: ⟦Q 82:1.10⟧Self-control, more and more self-control, is the ever-increasing demand of advancing mankind.⟦/Q⟧ (82:1.10)
082:26: The history of the evolution of marriage is the history of regulating sex through social, religious, and civil restrictions. Nature compels only the reproduction of the species and leaves the consequences to society, and so an endless struggle arises between basic instinct and evolving ethics (82:2.1). The early races had hardly any regulation, but ancient peoples must always be judged in the light of the mores of their own times (82:2.2). As soon as social groups formed, marriage standards began to develop (82:2.3).
082:27: Even the crude early taboos helped bring peace, order, and industry by keeping the sexes apart, and from them arose the customs of dress, ornament, and religious practice, as well as the ideas of vice, crime, and sin (82:2.4). Women were always bound by more taboos than men, and married women were marked off by signs such as the style of their hair, the veil, and the ring (82:2.5).
082:29: Marriage is society's institutional response to the ever-present biologic tension toward self-reproduction (82:3.1). The standards of marriage are an index of the strength of the mores of an age and of the health of civil government, and the races that honored and practiced marriage evolved higher and survived in greater numbers (82:3.3).
082:34: The mores and laws that regulate mating
082:36: The secret and personal relations of man and woman
082:38: In primitive times marriage was the price of social standing, and sometimes it was regarded as a social, religious, or political duty (82:3.4). A bridegroom went through tests such as feats of stealing, athletic contests, riddles, or a year of living with his wife's family, and a bride had to prove her capacity for hard work and childbearing (82:3.5-3.7). The belief that one who did not marry could not enter the spirit world led even to child marriages and to marriages of the dead, and widows were sometimes killed at their husbands' graves (82:3.8, 3.12).
082:39: Many tribes allowed trial marriage until pregnancy occurred. The book explains that this was not license but a sincere attempt to make sure of fertility. And it says that modern couples who marry with the thought of divorcing when convenient are in fact entering a trial marriage, one far below the honest venture of their ancestors (82:3.14-3.15).
082:49: In primitive society marriage was more a business investment than a romance, and parents and elders arranged it for the good of the group. The book says that thanks to these property mores, the marriages of early tribes lasted longer than those of many modern peoples (82:4.1-4.2). A woman was at first her father's property and was then handed over to her husband, and adultery was regarded as stealing the husband's property (82:4.3).
082:50: Modern sex jealousy is not innate but a product of evolved mores. Primitive man was not jealous of his wife; he was simply guarding his property (82:4.4). The chastity taboo also began in the property mores, and as a maiden became a commercial asset to her father, the custom of paying a bride price arose (82:4.5).
082:52: Early on, primitive man observed that mating with other groups improved the offspring. Inbreeding was not always bad, but outbreeding was generally better, and so the mores gradually came to forbid relations between close kin (82:5.1-5.2). On the other hand, religion, the preservation of property, and the guarding of trade secrets long encouraged endogamy (82:5.3).
082:65: Peace, alliances, nation building, cultural exchange
082:67: The book says that there is no biologic instinctive aversion to marriage between kin of any degree; the restrictions are wholly a matter of taboo (82:5.5). Exogamy lessened hostility between tribes and produced alliances, becoming a promoter of peace, and together with trade and adventure it greatly aided the cross-fertilization of cultures (82:5.9). Cases in which even in-laws with no blood relationship were forbidden show that these taboos were sociologic, not biologic (82:5.10).
082:69: The book says there are no pure races in the world today. The yellow and black races have also mixed much with other races now vanished, and the so-called white race is mixed to some degree with all the other races (82:6.1). The book also explains that the primary and secondary Sangik races each had desirable traits, and that biologically the secondary races were in some respects superior (82:6.2, 6.10).
082:70: The book holds that today's prejudice against racial mixture comes mainly from social and cultural prejudice. The crossing of different good stocks increases vigor and creative potential, and the danger of gross disharmonies from mixing human stocks has been greatly exaggerated (82:6.5, 6.7-6.8). The book's conclusion is that mankind's real danger lies not in racial mixture but in the unrestricted multiplication of the degenerate strains found in every people (82:6.11).
082:79: Mostly social and cultural prejudice rather than biology (82:6.7)
082:82: Paper 82 shows that marriage is not an institution handed down complete from heaven but one shaped by a long wrestling between instinct and ethics. The mating instinct led even selfish people to put the welfare of the species first, and crude taboos and mores gradually brought that power under control. Property held marriage steady, religion moralized it, and exogamy opened the way to peace between tribes. Even today's ideas of jealousy and chastity are products of this long history. And at the end of all this struggle, the greatest glory mankind has won is the home. That is why this paper calls again and again for self-control and urges us to preserve the home as the chief institution of education and civilization.
082:87: The sex urge carries on the species and demands ever more self-control
082:89: Crude taboos produced order and began the evolution of marriage
082:91: Marriage standards are an index of the strength of an age's mores
082:93: Property stabilized marriage, and religion moralized it
082:95: Exogamy opened the way to peace, alliances, and cultural exchange
082:97: There are no pure races, and objections to mixture are mainly social prejudice
082:100: Marriage grew up through a long struggle between instinct and ethics, and the highest glory that struggle produced is the home.
083:1: How did marriage, which began in coercion and bargaining, arrive at the ideal of pair marriage between one man and one woman?
083:4: In Paper 82 we saw how the mating instinct grew into marriage by way of taboos, mores, and ideas of property. Now Paper 83 looks concretely at the forms marriage has passed through as a social institution. Starting from the loose unions of the horde and going through many variations, marriage finally arrived at the union of one man and one woman that establishes a home of the highest social order: pair marriage (83:0.1).
083:5: Marriage has faced many crises and has received much help from property and religion. But the real force that forever safeguards marriage and the home is the simple fact that men and women, whether the most primitive savages or the most cultured people, will not live without each other (83:0.2). The book says that sex hunger became the hidden agent that civilized the savage, leading selfish human beings into self-denial and the responsibilities of the home (83:0.3).
083:6: By what process, then, did courtship and betrothal, bride price and dowry, wedding customs and plural marriages lead on to pair marriage? And what should marriage today learn from them?
083:8: ⟦Q 83:6.8⟧Marriage, which began in crude coercion, is gradually evolving into a magnificent institution of self-culture, self-control, self-expression, and self-perpetuation.⟦/Q⟧ (83:6.8)
083:12: Marriage is the mechanism society has devised to regulate the many human relationships that arise from the fact of two sexes (83:1.1). The home that comes from marriage, together with the property mores, stabilizes marriage, and pride, duty, and religious convictions add their strength. But marriages are hardly made in heaven. Marriage is an institution of society, not a department of the church; religion should influence it greatly, but it should not monopolize it (83:1.4).
083:17: Keeps the relations of men and women within the framework of society
083:18: 2. Regulating descent, inheritance, succession, and social order
083:19: The older, original function of marriage
083:21: Primitive marriage was mainly industrial in character; husband and wife grew attached by living and working together. As Andite blood and the mores of civilization were added, marriage has become increasingly mutual, romantic, ethical, and idealistic (83:1.5).
083:23: In primitive society marriages were arranged by parents, and on the way to free choice there were matchmakers. Marriage was at first a group affair, then a family matter, and only recently an individual adventure (83:2.1). Just as robbery came before trade, marriage by capture came before marriage by contract, and mock elopement, mock capture, and the custom of carrying the bride over the threshold are traces of it (83:2.2-2.3).
083:24: As civilization advanced, women came to take a larger and larger part in every stage of courtship and marriage (83:2.4). The book explains that the growth of love, romance, and personal choice in courtship was a contribution of the Andites (83:2.5). Betrothal was at first regarded as equal to marriage, and the sex taboos during betrothal were established by religion only recently (83:2.6).
083:36: The ancients did not trust love and promises; they thought a lasting union had to be guaranteed by the security of property. So the purchase price of a wife was a deposit the husband would lose in case of divorce or desertion (83:3.1). This did not mean daughters were sold like cattle; labor could take the place of payment, and elders sometimes had excessive demands lowered (83:3.2).
083:37: As civilization advanced, fathers did not like to appear to be selling their daughters, so they gave the couple gifts equal to the price received, and when the bride price disappeared these gifts became the dowry (83:3.3). The dowry symbolizes the bride's independence and shows how far things had moved from the days of slave wives (83:3.4).
083:43: From the groom's side to the bride's father
083:44: From the bride's side to the couple
083:53: The wedding ceremony arose because marriage was originally not a decision of two people alone but an affair of the community (83:4.1). In days without records, many people had to witness it so that property and the status of children would be known (83:4.2). At first it was no more than a public notice that two people intended to live together, but it gradually developed into the sharing of a meal and then into more elaborate celebrations (83:4.3).
083:54: The book explains that many of today's wedding customs are relics of the days when people feared spirits and ghosts (83:4.4-4.7). The insurance motive of guarding against marital failure led people to seek priests and magic, and this led directly to the modern church wedding. Within the last five hundred years church and state have taken over jurisdiction over marriage (83:4.9).
083:61: Driving off ghosts with fire and water
083:63: Hiding the bride from jealous spirits
083:64: A carpet laid to the altar
083:65: Keeping the bride's feet from touching the ground
083:67: Keeping them from looking happy and arousing the envy of spirits
083:70: Marriage moved out of the indiscriminate relations of the horde to the stage in which a woman had only one husband at a time, and then through group marriage to plural marriage in the forms of polygyny and polyandry. Polyandry was never common (83:5.1-5.3). The custom of raising up children by a dead brother's widow is a relic of the age when marriage was a family matter (83:5.4).
083:75: The chief wife, who held status
083:83: True polygyny, in which all wives and children were equal, was very rare; usually one wife of status headed the household (83:5.10). Concubinage, with one legal wife and several concubines, was a stepping stone toward monogamy (83:5.12). The number of wives depended on a man's ability to support them, and the harem was meant to build up a kinship group that would uphold the throne (83:5.14-5.15).
083:85: Whatever its effect on individuals, monogamy is certainly best for children (83:6.1). The earliest monogamy arose from poverty; it was a cultural institution not natural to evolving man, yet it held great value for all the advanced races (83:6.2). By the time Michael came, the civilized world had attained a nearly theoretical monogamy, but that did not mean true pair marriage was actually practiced (83:6.3).
083:86: The book asks us not to forget those who find no mate within this institution. The favored majority should always be kind to their less fortunate neighbors (83:6.4-6.5). Pair marriage demands self-denial, so without self-control, the highest of virtues, it often fails (83:6.6). But monogamy fosters refined feelings, the refinement of moral character, and spiritual growth that are impossible in plural marriage, and it is best for the happiness of parents and the welfare of children (83:6.7-6.8).
083:88: ⟦Q 83:6.6⟧Monogamy always has been, now is, and forever will be the idealistic goal of human sex evolution.⟦/Q⟧ (83:6.6)
083:91: Early marriages were loose unions that could be ended at any time, and the marriages of primitive peoples were only about half satisfactory. The most common cause of divorce was barrenness, and it was always blamed on the wife (83:7.1-7.2). The bride price and the dowry greatly reduced divorce by property penalties, and many marriages today are also stabilized by this property element (83:7.3).
083:92: The book diagnoses that marriage is temporarily shaken because the idealistic but highly individualistic motive of love has suddenly replaced the older motive of property (83:7.5). The real test of marriage is the constant intimacy of family life, and young people used to self-indulgence find it hard to succeed in a lifelong partnership of devotion (83:7.6). Overly romantic courtship and the lack of education for marriage increase divorce, and so long as that is the case divorce serves as a social safety valve that prevents worse things (83:7.7-7.8).
083:94: Marriage, which culminates in the home, is man's most exalted institution, but it is essentially human and should never have been called a sacrament (83:8.1). Marriage cannot be compared with the relationship of the Adjuster to man or of Michael to his human brothers (83:8.2-8.3). The very fact that marriage can be dissolved shows that God is not the one who joins the union (83:8.4).
083:95: Nevertheless, there is an ideal of marriage on the spheres on high as well. On the capitals of the local systems the Material Sons and Daughters actually portray the height of the union of man and woman for bearing and rearing children, and the ideal mortal marriage is humanly sacred (83:8.5). Young people's idealization of marriage should not be crushed, but it should be tempered with a little disillusionment by learning the realities of marriage beforehand (83:8.6-8.7). Marriage is not a relationship in which each possesses the whole personality of the other, but a social partnership of man and woman that grows under the mores and the laws (83:8.8).
083:97: ⟦Q 83:8.5⟧After all, the ideal mortal marriage is humanly sacred.⟦/Q⟧ (83:8.5)
083:100: Paper 83 shows that marriage has come a long way from its beginnings in capture, bargaining, and magical rites. The bride price became the dowry; group marriage and plural marriage moved through concubinage toward monogamy; and the one who decides on marriage shifted from the group to the family and then to the individual. But today, with individual love having suddenly replaced the motive of property, marriage faces a new test. The book tells us neither to exalt marriage into a sacrament nor to throw it away lightly. Marriage is a human institution, but pair marriage nurtured with self-control and devotion is best for children and helps souls grow, and such a marriage is humanly sacred.

083:107: The decision to marry passed from the group to the family and then to the individual
083:109: The bride price was a deposit, and the dowry meant the bride's independence

083:117: The real test of marriage is the constant intimacy of family life
083:119: Marriage is not a sacrament, but the ideal marriage is humanly sacred
083:122: Marriage is an institution made by humans, but pair marriage nurtured with self-control and devotion is humanly sacred.
084:1: Why is the home man's greatest achievement and the only hope for the survival of civilization?
084:4: In Paper 83 we saw how marriage passed through capture, bargaining, and plural marriage to reach the ideal of pair marriage. Now Paper 84 turns to the fruit of that marriage: family life. Material necessity founded marriage, sex hunger embellished it, religion sanctioned it, and the state regulated it. And in later times evolving love has come to glorify marriage as the creator of the home, the most useful and sublime institution of civilization (84:0.1).
084:5: Individuals come and go, but the family is the enduring agent in social evolution, and the home is the channel through which the river of culture and knowledge flows from one generation to the next (84:0.2). That is why, the book says, home building should be the center and essence of all education (84:0.1).
084:6: By what process, then, did the home come to be what it is now? And within it, what should man and woman, parents and children, be to one another?
084:8: ⟦Q 84:6.8⟧The family is man's greatest purely human achievement, combining as it does the evolution of the biologic relations of male and female with the social relations of husband and wife.⟦/Q⟧ (84:6.8)
084:12: Marriage did not grow out of sex relations. Primitive man could satisfy his sex urge without any responsibility, so he had no need of marriage (84:1.1). Woman, because of her attachment to her children, depended on man's co-operation, but what drew man into marriage was not love but hunger for food (84:1.2). Primitive people did not know the connection between sex relations and childbirth; they believed babies came from the spirit world and entered the woman's body (84:1.3).
084:13: Mother love, unlike marriage, comes not from the mores but from instinct. The mother love of all mammals is the gift of the adjutant mind-spirits, and its strength is greater the longer the period of infancy (84:1.6). The mother-child relationship is neither marriage nor the home, but it was the nucleus from which both sprang. The home came into being when a temporary partnership lasted long enough to raise children (84:1.8). A man and a woman co-operating are in most ways far superior to two men or two women (84:1.9).
084:15: Seeing the blood of childbirth, people believed that blood made the child, and from this arose the idea of blood kinship. Only the mother's line was certain, so at first all descent was reckoned through the mother (84:2.1). In the mother-family the wife's mother held the highest authority in the household, and the wife's brothers were more involved in family affairs than the husband (84:2.3).
084:27: Mother-child blood tie; the age of hunters
084:30: When herding gave men control of the food supply, the mother-family quickly disappeared. The scattered power of the mother's relatives could not compete with the power of the husband-father concentrated in one person (84:2.6). The book says this change was one of the most radical about-faces mankind has ever made (84:2.7).
084:32: What kept woman in married life was man's greater strength and the mores, and the family of pastoral society was built on the absolute authority of the father. Every society passed through this stage of patriarchal despotism (84:3.1). The book says that the blame for holding woman in low esteem does not rest on men alone. Motherhood was a handicap in the struggle for existence, and women's own admiration for warriors made them still more dependent (84:3.3-3.4).
084:33: Woman always had to work, and until modern times she was the real producer (84:3.7). Her first emancipation came when man agreed to take over farming, which had been woman's work, and when captives were made into farm laborers instead of being killed (84:3.8). The milk of domesticated animals greatly reduced infant mortality, and men brought the organizing techniques learned in hunting and war into agriculture, greatly improving the way the work was done (84:3.9-3.10).
084:35: In every age the status of woman is a measure of how far marriage has evolved as a social institution, and the progress of marriage is a gauge of the progress of civilization (84:4.1). Early woman was closer to property or a servant than a partner of man, yet wise women always had considerable influence in their own sphere (84:4.2-4.3). That many traditions, such as those of Eve and Pandora, blamed woman for evil shows that she was once widely distrusted (84:4.4).
084:36: Childbirth and menstruation were thought to make women unclean, and women were isolated for a week each month. The book says that even this foolish idea had a good side, giving overworked women a time of rest and meditation (84:4.6-4.9). It was a great advance when the husband's right to kill his wife at will was denied and when women became able to own property (84:4.10).
084:38: In self-perpetuation woman is man's equal, but in the partnership of self-maintenance she works at a disadvantage (84:5.1). Equality of the sexes is a beautiful concept, but it does not exist in nature, and woman's status has been in inverse proportion to the militarism of a nation and an age (84:5.3). Tribes that persisted in cruelty to women did not survive (84:5.4).
084:39: The book says that what truly emancipated woman was not religion but science. The modern factory made man's strength less necessary and freed woman from domestic slavery (84:5.7-5.8). Within the ideal of pair marriage woman has gained dignity, independence, equality, and education, and she now stands before the crucial test of proving herself worthy of them (84:5.10). Woman's rights are not man's rights; each sex excels in its own particular sphere, and they compete on equal terms only socially (84:5.11-5.14).
084:41: The reproductive urge brings man and woman together, but it does not make them stay together and build a home. Passion brings the two together, and the weaker parental instinct and the social mores bind them (84:6.1-6.2). Man and woman are two distinct varieties of the same species, so they can never fully understand each other (84:6.3). Yet woman has always been the moral standard-bearer and spiritual leader of mankind (84:6.4).
084:42: The book tells us to see the difference between the sexes not as a cause for worry but as a great benefit. Many creatures of the universe are created in dual phases of personality manifestation, and this dual union fosters versatility and helps overcome limitations (84:6.5). Men and women need each other not only in the mortal career but also in the morontia and spirit careers, and even in the Corps of the Finality they will stimulate and help one another (84:6.6).
084:49: Positive or aggressive and negative or retiring
084:52: ⟦Q 84:6.8⟧Marriage is the mother of all human institutions, for it leads directly to home founding and home maintenance, which is the structural basis of society.⟦/Q⟧ (84:6.8)
084:55: When the home is good, society is good. The cultural stability of the Jewish and Chinese peoples lies in their strong family groups (84:7.1). Marriage is now leaving the property stage and passing into the age of personality, and since woman is no longer property, new mores are appearing to stabilize marriage and the home (84:7.3).
084:60: The need for parental experience; the idea of procreating cosmic citizens
084:62: Procreation becomes voluntary, placed under human control
084:63: ⟦Q 84:7.6⟧3. The new function of pleasure lures⟦/Q⟧
084:64: Modern people refuse to bear unwanted children
084:66: Those with weak parental instinct leave fewer descendants
084:68: The home as a partnership of one man and one woman began more definitely in the days of Dalamatia, about half a million years ago, and Adam and Eve, as a couple working side by side in the Garden, showed mankind a new ideal (84:7.8). The large families of ancient times did not necessarily come from affection (84:7.11).
084:70: Why ancient people wanted many children
084:87: The book explains that rearing children today has become harder because of racial mixture, artificial and superficial education, and the frequent absence of parents (84:7.21-7.24). Bringing a child into the world is not a parent's right but the supreme responsibility of human existence, and a child's respect grows naturally out of loving care and training (84:7.25-7.26). Any attempt to hand over parental responsibility to the state or the church would be suicidal to civilization (84:7.27). The book urges a return to free and frank family councils like those of the Andites, and it says the home is the progenitor of true morality (84:7.29-7.30).
084:89: True parents portray to their children the first of a long series of ascending disclosures of the love of the Paradise parent of all universe children. (84:7.30)
084:92: The greatest threat to family life is the rising tide of self-gratification, the modern pleasure mania (84:8.1). Marriage is the one institution that embraces all three great motives of human society, but because the mores never established a distinct institution for self-gratification, all institutions have become permeated by pleasure seeking (84:8.1-8.2).
084:101: No distinct institution — it permeates all institutions
084:103: The longings of the soul are not satisfied by physical pleasures, and even pouring out art, music, and ornament cannot by themselves exalt the soul or nourish the spirit (84:8.4). This does not mean pleasure should be abandoned. Wholesome play, rest, and recreation all have value, and mankind deserves to enjoy the pleasures that are the fruit of its long struggle. But if pleasure destroys marriage and the home, the price paid is far too high (84:8.5-8.6).
084:105: Paper 84 shows how the home began in hunger for food and the instinct of motherhood and came down to us through the mother-family and the father-family. Along the way woman long carried a heavy burden, and science and industry unexpectedly brought her emancipation. The book sees the difference between the sexes not as a problem to be removed but as a gift by which the two help each other forever, and it exalts the home as the mother of all institutions and the progenitor of true morality. Parenthood is not a right but the highest responsibility, and good parents give their children their first glimpse of the love of the Paradise parent. So the task of our civilization today is to guard this home so that pleasure does not tear it down.

085:1: How does human worship, which once served stones, trees, and the sun, come to turn toward the God of nature?
085:4: In Paper 84 we saw how marriage and the home grew into man's greatest achievement. Now, beginning with Paper 85, we look at where another deep human institution, religion, began. Primitive religion was a natural product of evolution with a biologic origin, apart from morals or spiritual influences. The higher animals have fears but no illusions, and so no religion; man creates primitive religion out of his fears and his illusions (85:0.1).
085:5: The primitive forms of worship appeared long before man formed any concept worth calling religion, and their objects were things of nature that were close at hand or that stood out strikingly (85:0.2). Man has worshiped everything on earth, even himself, and still today we call what we cannot explain an act of God or a mysterious providence (85:0.4).
085:6: What, then, has man worshiped, one thing after another, and how will that fearful awe grow into true religion?
085:8: ⟦Q 85:6.3⟧Evolutionary religion creates its gods in the image and likeness of mortal man; revelatory religion seeks to evolve and transform mortal man into the image and likeness of God.⟦/Q⟧ (85:6.3)
085:12: The first thing evolving man worshiped was stone. Jacob slept on a stone and anointed it, and Rachel hid sacred stones in her tent (85:1.1). Stones that suddenly appeared in a field, rocks that looked like animals, and above all meteors falling through the sky made a deep impression on early man (85:1.2). But people did not always regard the stone itself as a god; such fetishes were often symbols of the real object of worship (85:1.3).
085:13: Stones with holes were believed to heal disease, and today's gravestones are surviving symbols of the stone images and idols of old (85:1.4). After stone worship came hill worship. As people came to believe that gods lived in the mountains, high places became sacred; caves were thought of as the underworld of evil spirits, and mountains as the abode of good spirits and gods (85:1.5).

086:1: Before revelation came, why and how did man come to have religion?
086:4: In Paper 85 we saw the origins of worship, as primitive man revered stones and trees, animals and the sky. Now Paper 86 follows how that worship urge grew into religion. The evolution of religion described in this paper does not depend on revelation. The normal functioning of the human mind under the guidance of the sixth and seventh adjutant mind-spirits is quite enough for this development to take place (86:0.1).
086:5: At first man simply feared the forces of nature. Then, as nature was personalized, spiritualized, and finally deified in human consciousness, that fear gradually became religious (86:0.2). Chance and misfortune, inexplicable death, and ancestors appearing in dreams became stepping stones along that way.
086:6: This primitive religion, born of fear, was full of mistaken ideas. How, then, could it become a preparation that led man toward ethics and true spiritual experience?
086:8: The divine Adjusters have ever since labored to transmute God-fear into God-love. (86:7.6)
086:12: Besides the natural worship urge, early religion was rooted in man's experience of chance, of good luck and bad luck. The results of the hunt varied from day to day, and in a life lived on the edge of a cliff, misfortune was a large factor (86:1.1). Primitive man struggled not for a standard of living but for existence itself, and the dread of unseen calamity overshadowed every joy. A run of good luck was even feared as a sign that disaster was coming (86:1.2).
086:13: Existence itself was a gamble. Primitive man swung between the longing to get something for nothing and the fear of getting nothing for his efforts (86:1.4). It was the same for the later herders and farmers. Everything beyond their control—drought, floods, hail, pests—was regarded as good or bad luck (86:1.5).
086:18: The results of the hunt, which varied from day to day
086:20: Kept the same view of chance and luck
086:22: Drought, floods, hail, storms, pests, disease, heat, and cold
086:25: Primitive man constantly asked, "Who is troubling me?" When he could find no material cause for his suffering, he settled on a spirit explanation, and so religion was born of the fear of the mysterious and the awe of the unseen (86:2.2). His mind was logical but short of ideas, so whenever one event followed another he took it as cause and effect. As a result, nature and chance were personalized as ghosts and spirits, and finally as gods (86:2.3).
086:26: The text puts its finger sharply on this attitude. To keep attributing things hard to understand to supernatural causes is a lazy and convenient way of avoiding hard intellectual work. But exploring the phenomena of life sooner or later destroys belief in chance, and a universe of law and order, where every effect is preceded by a cause, takes its place (86:2.5). Not all religion, however, came from animism; other supernatural concepts also led to worship (86:2.7).
086:28: ⟦Q 86:2.5⟧Thus is the fear of existence replaced by the joy of living.⟦/Q⟧ (86:2.5)
086:31: Death was the greatest shock to evolving man, the most perplexing combination of chance and mystery. Not the sanctity of life but the shock of death inspired fear and so fostered religion (86:3.1). Among savages death usually came by violence, so a death without violence seemed all the more mysterious. That every race has legends of people who did not die is a trace of the early attitude that saw death as a kind of calamity (86:3.2).
086:32: At first all illness and natural death were believed to be caused by spirit influence. This idea lingered even in later complex theologies, giving rise to doctrines such as original sin and the fall of man (86:3.3). Realizing his helplessness before nature and his weakness before disease and death, the savage placed the cause in a supermaterial world and began to seek help there (86:3.4).
086:34: The idea that something remains after death arose from a chance combination of everyday events and ghost dreams. When several members of a tribe dreamed of a departed chief at the same time, they took it as proof that the chief had returned in some form (86:4.1). The breath that looked like a cloud on a cold day was also of great interest. Breath was the sign that set the living apart from the dead, and from the ideas of breath and dreams came the most primitive concept of the human soul, the ghost (86:4.3). Breath without a body was a spirit, a ghost (86:4.4).
086:35: This early doctrine of survival did not mean immortality. People who could not count beyond twenty could not grasp eternity, so they thought in terms of repeated incarnations (86:4.5). The belief that a person dies three to seven times is a remnant of Adam's teaching about the mansion worlds (86:4.6). At first the future life was pictured as a place like this world without bad luck; heaven and hell were conceived later (86:4.7). Ideas about the destiny of the soul differed from people to people (86:4.8).

086:42: The ghost returned to the homeland of the ancestors
086:44: Soul and body remain together — tomb building and preserving the body
086:46: A phantom replica went down to Sheol and could not return
086:49: The nonmaterial part of man has been called ghost, spirit, shade, phantom, specter, and later soul. To early man the soul was his dream double, exactly like himself except that it could not be touched (86:5.1). As civilization advances, such superstitious ideas of the soul disappear, and man comes to understand the soul as the joint creation of the God-knowing mind and the indwelling Thought Adjuster. This concept depends on revelation and personal religious experience (86:5.2).
086:50: The ancients believed the soul could leave the body in various ways, as fragrance leaves a flower (86:5.4-5.8). A sneeze was thought to be a failed attempt by the soul to escape, so a blessing was said after it, and a sleeping person was awakened slowly to give the soul time to return (86:5.9-5.10). Moses forbade the belief that God speaks through dreams, and the text says Moses was right, since spiritual personalities do not communicate through ordinary dreams (86:5.11).
086:63: The soul was usually identified with the breath, but some peoples believed it lived in the head, the hair, the heart, the liver, the blood, or the fat (86:5.15). Breath, shadows, and reflections in water were also taken as evidence of the soul (86:5.13-5.14). Ideas about the number of souls varied as well (86:5.16-5.17).

086:72: Vegetative soul (stomach), animal soul (heart), intellectual soul (head)

086:77: ⟦Q 86:6.1⟧Man inherited a natural environment, acquired a social environment, and imagined a ghost environment.⟦/Q⟧ And in response to each environment institutions arose (86:6.1). The imagined spirit world was accepted as real at a very early time, and it changed forever the mental and moral life of all mankind (86:6.2).
086:88: If people believed that angry ghosts brought bad luck and pleased ones brought good luck, they had to adjust their conduct accordingly. It was then that the idea of right and wrong was born, long before any revelation (86:6.6). There followed a long and wasteful struggle to appease discontented spirits, but the cost was worth it, for in that process human ethics was born (86:6.7). The text's remark that each generation laughs at the superstitions of its ancestors while repeating errors its descendants will laugh at calls for humility from us today as well (86:6.5).
086:90: Primitive religion was insurance against the dangers of the forest. The savage willingly paid the costly premiums of fear, superstition, and gifts to the priests (86:7.1). Modern society has moved this insurance function into the economic realm, and religion is rising from a system of insurance against bad luck to higher philosophic levels (86:7.2). Even so, the old religion kept man from sinking into fatalism or hopeless pessimism, because it led him to believe he could do something to change his fate (86:7.3).

086:101: The text adds one more warning. In giving up the error of blaming spirits for the ups and downs of life, people are taking up a similar error: blaming every inequality solely on political, social, or industrial causes. Only an understanding of the facts and wise action within the laws of nature is the antidote for so-called chance misfortunes (86:7.4). And primitive religion, by the power of false fear, prepared the soil of the mind for the bestowal of the Thought Adjuster (86:7.6).

086:106: Paper 86 does not hide that the beginnings of religion were anything but lofty. The good and bad luck of the hunt, inexplicable death, ancestors appearing in dreams, and cloud-like breath gave rise to a world of ghosts and spirits, and for ages man poured enormous effort into appeasing that imagined world. Yet out of that very fear grew the sense of right and wrong, human ethics was born, and man held on to the hope that he could do something about his own destiny. Into the field of the mind plowed by false fear came the Thought Adjuster, who is still at work transforming God-fear into God-love.

087:1: How can rituals that grew out of the fear of the dead become the skeleton of true religion?
087:4: In Paper 86 we saw how a world of ghosts and spirits was imagined out of chance and death, dreams and breath. Now Paper 87 shows what man did in dealing with those imagined ghosts. The ghost cult arose to offset the hazards of bad luck, and its rituals were mostly negative—attempts to avoid, expel, or coerce ghosts. It was insurance against disaster, far removed from any investment in a higher future (87:0.1).
087:5: Mankind has struggled painfully with the ghost cult for ages, and nothing is more pitiful than the picture of man enslaved to the fear of ghosts. Yet this very fear drove mankind onto the path of religious evolution. Human imagination will never come to anchor until it reaches the concept of the true God (87:0.2).
087:6: In these cults so full of fear, deception, and waste, what is it, then, that we today should carry on?
087:8: ⟦Q 87:7.10⟧The cult is the skeletal structure around which grows the living and dynamic body of personal spiritual experience—true religion.⟦/Q⟧ (87:7.10)
087:12: Death was dreaded because it meant that one more ghost had been set free from a body. Ghosts were most feared during the transition period from the moment of death until they departed for ghostland (87:1.1). The savage believed ghosts had supernatural power but not supernatural intelligence, so he tried to deceive them by every trick he could think of. The text remarks pointedly that even civilized people expect to fool an all-knowing God with outward displays of piety (87:1.2).
087:13: A house where someone had died was torn down or avoided, and this fear held back the building of durable homes and permanent villages (87:1.3). People believed that sleeping beside a corpse meant death, so they stayed awake all night, and they kept lights burning so the body would not be left in darkness (87:1.4). There were many ways of deceiving ghosts (87:1.5).
087:17: Carrying the body out through a hole made in the wall
087:18: Confusing the ghost so it could not return
087:19: Returning from the funeral by a different road
087:22: Keeping the ghost from recognizing the survivors
087:24: At first a disguise; later respect and appeasement
087:27: The negative program of placating ghosts long preceded any positive program of coercing or supplicating spirits. Man's first acts of worship were not acts of reverence but of defense (87:2.1). Funeral rites came from efforts to send the ghost off to its future home, and funeral sermons from the effort to teach the new ghost the way there. It was believed that "laying" a ghost took from three days to a year (87:2.3).
087:28: Mourning was a ritual not of grief but of fear. Professional mourners were hired, and weeks or months every year were wasted in unproductive mourning (87:2.5). The names of the dead became taboo, impoverishing language (87:2.6). The book calmly records that, in the belief that ghosts wanted wives and servants, there were even customs of burying people with the dead or putting them to death (87:2.7-2.8). Tools and property were also broken or burned and sent along, and civilization made a great advance when inheritance by kin took the place of this (87:2.10).
087:32: Sending real objects and people with the dead
087:37: Mourning born of respect and a sense of loss
087:40: The advancing ghost cult inevitably led to ancestor worship. Ancestor worship was the connecting link between ordinary ghosts and the higher spirits, the evolving gods, and the early gods were simply glorified dead humans (87:3.1). The custom of adoption, too, was meant to make sure that someone would offer sacrifices for one's soul after death (87:3.3).
087:41: Most tribes held a yearly feast for all souls. The Romans kept twelve ghost feasts a year, and when half the year was given to such ceremonies, one emperor tried to reduce the feast days to 135 (87:3.4). As people imagined ghosts moving up to higher levels, the cult also developed into the worship of spirits and gods (87:3.5).
087:43: For a long time many tribes believed in only one kind of ghost: when it was pleased, good luck came, and when it was angry, bad luck came (87:4.1). Then the idea of two classes of spirits, good and bad, arose independently all over the world (87:4.3-4.4). This dualism was one of the most important truth discoveries in religious evolution, because while explaining both good and bad luck, it allowed belief in supermortal beings whose conduct was consistent (87:4.5).

087:50: Good and bad spirits — each acting consistently
087:52: The idea of consistent supermortal forces

087:56: But the cost was high too. This doctrine made it difficult for religionists to conceive of the unity of the cosmos, and the gods of evolutionary religion were always pitted against the forces of darkness (87:4.6). The heart of the tragedy is that when this idea took root, there were no evil spirits in the world at all. Such a situation arose only after the Caligastia rebellion and lasted only until Pentecost (87:4.7).
087:58: Primitive man believed that spirits had only rights and no duties, and that humans had only duties and no rights. Even after offering sacrifices to every known spirit he did not feel safe, so he made one more offering to "⟦Q 87:5.1⟧the unknown gods⟦/Q⟧" (87:5.1). Religion was man's way of adjusting to the illusion of the mystery of chance, and the worship of spirits was a prosperity insurance policy (87:5.2). Since good spirits were thought to go about their business anyway, people paid far more attention to the bad ghosts (87:5.3).
087:59: Prosperity was believed to arouse the envy of evil spirits, and the fear of the evil eye spread almost worldwide (87:5.4). So customs arose of speaking lightly of success and disclaiming praise; early modesty was not self-belittling but an attempt to deceive envious spirits. In time this developed into civilized modesty and courtesy (87:5.6-5.7). On the other hand, the custom of hiding beauty long held back the development of art (87:5.7).

087:66: Correct conduct and ritual that enlist the spirits in one's interests
087:68: A right understanding of spirits — the right view of life and death
087:70: The will of the spirits was sought through omens, oracles, and signs, and interpreted by divination, prophecy, sorcery, ordeals, and astrology (87:5.9). The ancients sought to know the future not out of curiosity but to avoid bad luck. Man is very slow to give up the old methods that have brought him this far (87:5.14).
087:72: Once people arrived at the idea of good and bad spirits, ritual no longer stopped at warding off bad luck but took on the active character of seeking good luck. Man began to devise weapons for forcing the co-operation of the spirits (87:6.2). The first defenses were aimed at ghosts, and many techniques for frightening and driving them off arose (87:6.3-6.10).

087:91: Shouting, bells and drums, foul smells, and frightening figures were used to drive off ghosts (87:6.11). Water was the supreme protection; baptism and religious bathing came from this, and bathing became a hygienic habit only relatively recently (87:6.12). Exorcism was the use of one spirit to drive out another, and the primitive curse was a means of subduing lesser spirits (87:6.13). Self-denial, vows, and fasting were also thought sure ways of coercing spirits, leading on to asceticism (87:6.16). Even modern people swear oaths and knock on wood, still trying to bargain with the gods (87:6.17).
087:93: The cult persisted because it provided symbols that preserve and stimulate moral sentiments and religious loyalties (87:7.1). Yet while it preserved sentiment, the cult was also the greatest obstacle to social reconstruction and spiritual progress (87:7.2). A religious cult cannot be manufactured artificially; it must grow (87:7.3). The early Christian cult was the most effective and enduring of rituals, but in the age of science it lost its vitality as it lost its fundamental doctrines (87:7.4).

When the religion of Jesus is restated, it too will need new symbols, founded on the fatherhood of God and embracing the ideal of the brotherhood of man (87:7.6). Yet in the course of it, the dualism of good and bad spirits gave rise to the truth of consistent supermortal forces, and gestures meant to deceive spirits were refined into modesty and courtesy. In the end this paper says that the cult itself is not bad. Hardened ritual blocks progress, but a living cult that grows out of applied love becomes the skeleton around which personal spiritual experience grows.

088:1: How did the belief that feared spirit-indwelt objects lead all the way to scriptures, national flags, and science?
088:4: In Paper 87 we saw the ghost cults, in which man tried to deceive, placate, and coerce ghosts. Now Paper 88 moves on to the belief that those spirits dwell in objects, animals, and people. The doctrine of spirit possession—that a spirit enters an inanimate object, an animal, or a human being—is fetishism. Quite logically, the savage worshiped not so much the fetish itself as the spirit he believed dwelt within it (88:0.1).
088:5: At first the spirit in a fetish was thought to be the ghost of a dead person, but later higher spirits were believed to dwell there. In this way the fetish cult gathered into one all the primitive ideas of ghosts, souls, spirits, and demon possession (88:0.2).
088:6: In what form, then, does the belief that feared pebbles and nail parings remain today, and how did it bear the fruit of science?

088:12: Primitive man always made fetishes of things out of the ordinary, and chance was the origin of many fetishes. A volcano became a fetish but not a mountain; a comet became a fetish but not a star (88:1.1). The first fetishes were peculiarly marked pebbles, and ever since, man has been looking for "sacred stones." Fire and water were also early fetishes, and fire worship and the belief in holy water survive even now (88:1.2).
088:13: When a plant or an animal became a fetish, eating it became taboo (88:1.3, 1.5). Certain days of the week and certain numbers were fetishes too (88:1.6). Parts of the body such as spittle, hair, nails, and the navel cord also became fetishes, and a preserved navel cord was mankind's first toy (88:1.8). A genius was regarded as a fetish personality indwelt by a wise spirit, and so chiefs, kings, priests, and prophets came to wield unlimited authority (88:1.10).

088:22: Unlucky Friday and thirteen; lucky four

088:29: Ghosts were thought to like to dwell in objects they had owned in life, and this explains the efficacy of relics. Belief in relics grew out of the ancient fetish cult. Calling fetishes and magic pagan while accepting relics and miracles is a trace of this (88:2.1-2.2). The first images were memorials to the great dead, and idols were a refined form of fetishism (88:2.4).
088:30: Moses tried to curb fetish worship by adding the second commandment. This commandment hindered the development of art, but it lessened fetish worship (88:2.5). In the end, though, words—especially those regarded as the word of God—became fetishes, and scriptures became prisons that confine the spiritual imagination of man (88:2.6). Fetishized doctrine delivers man into the grip of bigotry, fanaticism, and intolerance (88:2.7).

088:34: Opening a sacred book at random and letting the verse that appears decide a life choice, or laying a hand on that book to swear an oath, is also a refined form of fetishism (88:2.8). Even so, to have come from fearing a chief's nail parings to revering a collection of moral wisdom sifted over the centuries is real progress (88:2.9).

088:48: Fetishism ran through all the primitive cults, from sacred stones through idolatry and nature worship to totemism (88:3.1). Totemism is a combination of social custom and religious observance. The totem was the symbol of the group and also its god; it was the clan personified. The totem finally developed into the flags, the national symbols, of modern peoples (88:3.2).

088:55: A flag never allowed to touch the ground

088:61: The text says that man has even fetishized democracy. People think the opinion of one individual is of little worth, yet when many people's identical judgments are gathered into "public opinion," they exalt it as the arbiter of justice and the standard of righteousness (88:3.4).
088:63: Civilized man meets the problems of his real environment through science, but the savage tried to solve the problems of a fictitious spirit environment through magic. Magic was the art of gaining or forcing the co-operation of spirits by using fetishes or more powerful spirits (88:4.1). Surprisingly, the aims of magic and science are the same (88:4.2-4.5).

088:72: Mankind made its painful way from magic to science not by meditation and reason but through long experience. Starting in error and advancing in error, it backed its way to the threshold of truth, and only when the scientific method came did it turn to face forward (88:4.5). The fascination of early superstition was the mother of later scientific curiosity (88:4.6). The book records that, because natural death was not understood, several innocent people were sometimes executed for one person's death (88:4.7). Fear itself could kill, and so magic became all the more entrenched (88:4.8).
088:74: Since anything connected with the body could become a fetish, early magic centered on hair and nails. People buried their excrement, covered their spittle, and left no food scraps not for hygiene but for fear that an enemy might use these in magic (88:5.1). It was believed that mistreating or caring for an image would have the same effect on the real person (88:5.3). The customs of a new civilization—writing, printing, and pictures—were also long regarded as evil magic (88:5.4).
088:75: Names too were important in magic. A name was a separate entity, as precious as the soul and the shadow, and it could even be pawned for a loan. A person's real name was not told to strangers, and so nicknames arose (88:5.5).
088:80: Signing one's name to a promissory note
088:83: Buying a new name from the chief
088:84: Investing to obtain titles and degrees
088:87: In magic, "medicine" meant not healing but mystery (88:6.1). There was public magic, performed by medicine men and priests for the whole tribe, and private magic, performed by witches and wizards to harm enemies, and the ideas of good and bad spirits led to white and black magic (88:6.2). Some incantations eventually developed into prayers, and prayer, together with sacrifice, gradually replaced magic (88:6.3).
088:88: Magic was a branch that grew from the tree of evolutionary religion and finally bore the fruit of the scientific age (88:6.5). But a world full of charms crushed individual initiative. Anyone whose harvest was larger than his neighbor's was suspected of luring the grain away by magic, and knowing too much was also dangerous (88:6.6). If modern education were to fail, people would return almost at once to belief in magic (88:6.7).
088:99: Urantia today is in the twilight zone of this intellectual evolution. Half the world is reaching out for the light of truth and the facts of science, while the other half lies in the arms of ancient superstition and thinly disguised magic (88:6.8).
088:101: Paper 88 shows how far the old belief that spirits dwell in objects has reached. Sacred stones and a chief's nail parings have changed into relics and scriptures, totems and medicine bags into flags and nations, spells and charms into public opinion and titles, and they are still with us today. Above all, when words become fetishes, scripture becomes a prison for the spiritual imagination, and doctrine delivers man to bigotry and intolerance. Yet this paper does not merely mock magic. The fascination of superstition was the mother of scientific curiosity, and magic was the cocoon that held science. Now the task before us is to shed that cocoon and move toward the light of truth.

089:1: How did man, who once appeased the gods with bloody sacrifices, arrive at forgiveness as the restoration of loyalty?
089:4: In Paper 88 we saw how deeply fetishes, charms, and magic ruled human life. Now Paper 89 follows the idea that man is in debt to the spirits. Primitive man regarded himself as owing a debt to the spirits and in need of redemption, and in time this concept developed into the doctrines of sin and salvation. The soul was thought to be born under the mortgage of original sin and to need redemption by a ransom (89:0.1).
089:5: The savage believed the spirits took satisfaction in seeing human misery and suffering, and he worried at first only about sins of commission and later about sins of omission as well. The whole sacrificial system grew up around these two ideas. Only advanced civilizations recognize a God who is consistently gentle and merciful (89:0.2).
089:6: Where, then, does this long road of taboo and renunciation, sacrifice and redemption finally lead, and how should we today understand sin and forgiveness?
089:8: ⟦Q 89:10.3⟧There is no real sin in the absence of conscious disloyalty to Deity.⟦/Q⟧ (89:10.3)
089:12: A taboo was the avoidance of certain acts in order to escape bad luck and not anger the spirit ghosts. At first taboos were nonreligious, but once they gained the sanction of ghosts or spirits they became lawmakers and institution builders. The taboo was the source of ceremonial standards and the beginning of primitive self-control, and for a long time it was the only social regulation (89:1.1).
089:13: The seven commandments of Dalamatia and Eden, and the ten commandments of the Hebrews, were all taboos in the form of "thou shalt not." Yet these codes brought real liberation by replacing thousands of outworn taboos, and they also promised a reward for obedience (89:1.4). Taboos were a heavy burden, but without them there could have been no civilized society to criticize primitive man. The achievement of self-control lifted mankind onto the steps of civilization (89:1.6-1.7).
089:18: Religious dietary laws, such as the taboo on pork
089:24: The seven commandments and the ten commandments
089:27: Religion developed from magic and ghosts, through spirits and fetishes, to taboos. Every primitive tribe had its tree of forbidden fruit that said, "⟦Q 89:2.1⟧Thou shalt not⟦/Q⟧" (89:2.1). When people imagined good and bad spirits and taboos gained religious sanction, the concept of sin appeared. Sin was the breaking of a taboo, and death was its penalty. Only through the concept of sin could primitive man understand natural death (89:2.2).
089:28: Sin was a deed, not a thought; it was ritual, not rational. The traditions of Eden strengthened the belief that man began in perfection and fell by breaking a taboo (89:2.3). Primitive law made vices into crimes, religion made them into sins, and hell was invented to explain the prosperity of the wicked (89:2.4). Confession and forgiveness also appeared early, but they were only a ritual of absolution and a public acknowledgment of uncleanness (89:2.5).
089:30: Renunciation was the next step in religious evolution. Fasting and the renunciation of bodily pleasures became customary, and property was regarded as a spiritual hindrance, so many sought poverty (89:3.1-3.2). Many of its forms were foolish, but all of this taught the savage self-control. Self-denial and self-control were the two greatest social gains of early evolutionary religion (89:3.3).
089:32: ⟦Q 89:3.3⟧Self-control gave man a new philosophy of life; it taught him the art of augmenting life's fraction by lowering the denominator of personal demands instead of always attempting to increase the numerator of selfish gratification.⟦/Q⟧ (89:3.3)
089:34: The ascetic cult tolerated marriage only as a lesser evil than fornication, and through Paul's personal views it found its way into Christian theology. Paul himself said this was a permission and not a command, but the idea led to a war on marriage and the home and to a celibate priesthood (89:3.6). Self-control is a better way than extreme self-denial, and Jesus did not teach these unreasonable views (89:3.7).
089:36: Primitive man measured the value of a sacrifice by the pain he suffered. The earliest sacrifices were pulling out hair or cutting the flesh, and as civilization advanced these were elevated into asceticism, fasting, and the doctrine of sanctification through suffering (89:4.1). At first sacrifice was an assessment levied by the ancestor spirits, and as the concept of original sin spread it developed into the doctrine of atonement for racial guilt (89:4.5).
089:43: Redemption, that is, paying off a debt
089:45: Replacing it with something else (a later development)
089:47: If renunciation was the negative form of placation, sacrifice was its positive form. The remnants of this placation, including praise, glorification, and even flattery, make up the forms of worship today (89:4.7). In the end people ate the material part of the offering, saying that the gods had already enjoyed its soul, and this gained the standing of a sacred meal, a communion (89:4.10).
089:49: The book explains that early cannibalism, though horrible to us today, was part of the social and religious structure of primitive society. It arose from necessity and persisted through superstition and ignorance (89:5.1). Since food was man's greatest need, it was thought to be the greatest need of spirits too (89:5.2). The book records that this practice was almost universal among the evolutionary races, but that it was absent among the original Andonites, the Nodites, and the Adamites (89:5.3).
089:50: The practice gradually died out through several stages. The parts eaten and the people who ate them were steadily restricted, and the taboo on cannibalism began in Dalamatia and slowly spread through the whole world. Finally, when human sacrifice was established, human flesh became the food of the gods alone, and people ate only a small ceremonial portion (89:5.8-5.15). Later, animals came into wide use as substitutes (89:5.16).

089:70: The book explains that human sacrifice was an indirect result of cannibalism as well as its cure. The practice was almost universal, and no race was wholly free of it (89:6.1-6.2). The Chaldeans were among the first to offer animals instead of humans at everyday occasions, and a Japanese emperor introduced clay images (89:6.2).
089:71: The most tragic example is the story of Jephthah and his only daughter. Having made a foolish vow as the price of victory, Jephthah offered his daughter as a sacrifice despite Moses' prohibition (89:6.3). There were also foundation sacrifices, in which people were buried when a new building was erected, and today's ceremony of placing mementos in a cornerstone is a remnant of this (89:6.4-6.6). The story of Abraham and Isaac, too, was not a strange idea to the people of that time (89:6.8).
089:73: Moses tried to end human sacrifice through a substitute, redemption. He made it possible to redeem land, property, and children by paying a fixed ransom. Groups that stopped sacrificing their firstborn soon enjoyed a great advantage over their neighbors (89:7.1). The book explains that human sacrifice changed into a number of forms (89:7.2-7.5).
089:78: Paying a ransom to the priests in place of a life
089:82: If they survived, the gods were thought to have preserved them
089:84: Sent away instead of killed — an origin of colonization
089:86: The book records that it led to temple prostitution
089:89: Redemption through sacrifice was a modification of human sacrifice, and later the offering of a part of the body took the place of a whole sacrifice. Hair, nails, and blood were offered, and circumcision too arose not from hygiene but from partial sacrifice (89:8.1-8.2). Tattooing is an artistic development of the practice of scarring the body (89:8.3).
089:90: At last sacrifice became joined to the idea of the covenant. The belief that the gods made covenants with men was a major step in stabilizing religion (89:8.4). Man could not conceive of a trustworthy God until he himself became trustworthy and moral (89:8.5). But early sacrifices and prayers were not true worship; they were bargaining with the gods and petitions for a deal (89:8.6-8.8).
089:92: ⟦Q 89:8.4⟧Law, a covenant, takes the place of luck, fear, and superstition.⟦/Q⟧ (89:8.4)
089:95: Over long ages the sacrificial rites advanced to higher and more symbolic levels and gave rise to the later sacramental rites. The ideas of ransom, redemption, and covenant developed into sacraments, and this evolution exerted a mighty socializing power (89:9.1). The sacrament of bread and wine took the place of the flesh and blood of the old sacrifices, and the Christian sacrament came from the Passover ceremony (89:9.2).
089:96: Paul built a new cult on "⟦Q 89:9.3⟧the blood of the everlasting covenant⟦/Q⟧." He may have burdened Christianity with needless teachings about blood and sacrifice, but he put an end once and for all to doctrines of redemption through human or animal sacrifice. This compromise shows that even revelation must submit to the gradual control of evolution (89:9.3). Today salvation through blood has become, at least, figurative and symbolic (89:9.4).
089:105: The priests alone tasted, then all shared the animal
089:107: Bread and wine — figurative and symbolic salvation
089:110: The ancients could be conscious of God's favor only through sacrifice, but modern man must find new ways to attain self-consciousness of salvation. The spiritual need is unchanged, but the old ways have been undermined by intellectual progress (89:10.1). So sin must be redefined as deliberate disloyalty to Deity (89:10.2). The feeling of guilt is only the awareness of having violated the mores; it does not necessarily mean sin (89:10.3).
089:123: Being able to feel guilt is not a brand that debases man, but the mark of a creature with potential greatness (89:10.4). Confession is a courageous repudiation of disloyalty and is essential to spiritual growth (89:10.5). And divine forgiveness need not be sought; it need only be received as the awareness that the loyalty relationship has been re-established (89:10.6).
089:125: ⟦Q 89:10.6⟧The forgiveness does not have to be sought, only received as the consciousness of re-establishment of loyalty relations between the creature and the Creator.⟦/Q⟧ (89:10.6)
089:128: Paper 89 follows to the end the road mankind has traveled in fearing sin and trying to pay its price. Taboo taught self-control, renunciation left the wisdom of reducing one's demands, and sacrifice rose from cannibalism to human sacrifice, to redemption and covenant, and finally to the symbolic sacrament. The road was dark and painful, but it was not in vain. Now this paper tells us to understand sin not as the breaking of a taboo but as conscious disloyalty to Deity. Forgiveness, then, is not something bought by paying a price; it is what a child who has returned to loyalty receives, upon realizing that the broken relationship has been restored.

090:1: What did the shamans and priests who claimed to stand between man and God block for mankind, and what did they leave behind?
090:4: In Paper 89 we saw how taboo, sacrifice, and atonement developed. Religious observances advanced from avoidance, exorcism, coercion, and propitiation to sacrifice, atonement, and redemption, and their techniques developed through fetishes into magic and miracles. As ritual grew more complex, it passed into the hands of medicine men, shamans, and priests (90:0.1).
090:5: At last the spirit world came to be regarded as unresponsive to ordinary people. As people came to believe that only special persons could gain the ear of the gods, religion entered an indirect stage (90:0.2). Evolutionary religion is born of an all-powerful fear and finally reaches the realization of the all-powerful love of the Universal Father, but between that beginning and its consummation lie the long ages of the shamans, who claimed to be intermediaries between man and God (90:0.3).
090:6: How, then, did these intermediaries gain power, how did they explain disease and death, and what have their rituals left to today's worship?
090:8: Religion eventually achieves the profoundly simple realization of an all-powerful love. (90:0.3)
090:12: The shaman was the ranking medicine man, the ceremonial fetishman, and the central personality of evolutionary religion. In many groups the shaman's authority surpassed that of the war chief, a sign of the church beginning to dominate the state (90:1.1). Since every abnormal phenomenon was thought to be spirit possession, marked mental or physical abnormality actually became a qualification for a medicine man (90:1.2).
090:13: Most shamans believed they were possessed by spirits, but many were clever frauds. Drugs, sleight of hand, ventriloquism, and hypnotism discovered by chance produced an air of mystery (90:1.3-1.4). But a shaman's reputation depended on visible results; if he failed and could not explain it away, he was demoted or executed. So the honest shamans died out early, and only the clever performers survived (90:1.5).
090:20: The shrewd, the clever, and the farsighted (90:1.6)
090:23: The rituals for calling up spirits were as elaborate as modern church services conducted in an ancient language. Shamans made great use of suggestion, but almost always negative suggestion. The shaman's chief function was not healing disease but knowing and managing the hazards of life (90:2.1). Casting lots, omens and portents, primitive astrology, and the interpretation of dreams were all their tools (90:2.4-2.5). Once, the person chosen by lot had to die; now he merely becomes "it" in a children's game (90:2.4).
090:28: Priests, seers, shamans, medicine men — the gods recognized by the tribe
090:30: Sorcerers, magicians, witches, necromancers — unrecognized spirits
090:32: Later, when witches became associated with the devil, the stage was set for much of the religious intolerance of relatively recent times (90:2.3). Through their fees the shamans built up great wealth, became the original aristocracy exempt from all tribal restrictions, and suppressed rivals by branding them witches (90:2.11-2.12). Yet in every age true prophets and teachers arose to expose shamanism (90:2.9). Primitive man feared the shaman but did not love him, and the respect paid to shamans actually shows how highly mankind valued wisdom (90:2.13).
090:34: Since primitive man thought that he and his environment responded directly to the whims of ghosts, it was natural for his religion to be absorbed in material problems. Since all disease and death were regarded as spiritual phenomena, it was inevitable that the shaman should also serve as physician and surgeon (90:3.1-3.2). The primitive mind was logical even when short of facts, and according to its level of understanding, five theories arose (90:3.3).
090:36: Theories of the cause of disease and death
090:39: A spirit lures the soul away — abandoning the sick unexpectedly served as quarantine
090:41: Obvious causes, such as war or beasts, were seen as natural events
090:43: The evil eye and the pointing bow — autopsies reduced accusations of witchcraft

090:49: The book records that there are still tribes that single out and kill someone whenever a nonviolent death occurs (90:3.6). The idea that disease is the wrath of God is still widespread even among civilized groups (90:3.8). But an understanding of aging and contagion is gradually erasing the fear of ghosts and gods as the inflicters of suffering (90:3.9).
090:51: ⟦Q 90:3.10⟧Evolution unerringly achieves its end: It imbues man with that superstitious fear of the unknown and dread of the unseen which is the scaffolding for the God concept.⟦/Q⟧ (90:3.10)
090:54: The whole life of the ancients was preventive, and their religion was in large part a technique for preventing disease. They had boundless faith in their remedies, and that faith was itself a powerful remedy (90:4.1). In societies that feared, avoided, and neglected the sick, the rise of priests and medicine men who undertook to treat disease was a great humanitarian advance (90:4.3).

090:61: Trephining the skull · setting fractures and dislocations · lancing boils · midwifery

090:69: The Greeks were the first to treat the sick in a truly rational way, and Greece and Egypt received their medical knowledge from the Euphrates valley (90:4.9). It is no accident that secret remedies lost their power once they became known. Secrecy is essential to fraud and superstition, but facts and truth welcome the light of understanding (90:4.9).
090:71: To the savage the essence of ritual lay in the perfection of its performance. Believing that only exact performance could coerce the spirits, the shamans developed into a priesthood that carried out rituals in minute detail. As a result, for tens of thousands of years endless rituals became an intolerable burden on every affair of life (90:5.1). Ritual is the technique of sanctifying custom; it creates and perpetuates myths (90:5.2).

090:82: Actual leaders of religious worship — later a hereditary caste
090:86: The priests heightened their authority by inspiring awe with ancient languages and mysterious hand movements, and the greatest danger is that ritual comes to take the place of religion itself (90:5.6). The priesthood slowed science and spiritual progress, but it contributed to the stability of civilization (90:5.7). The text admits that priests were a millstone around the neck of the races, yet it says that true religious leaders were of inestimable value in pointing the way to higher realities (90:5.8).
090:88: Paper 90 shines an honest light on the long age when intermediaries stood between man and God. Shamans took abnormality for inspiration, created mystery through trickery and suggestion, and amassed wealth and power. Their theories of disease were mostly wrong, and their endless rituals weighed life down. Yet even among them a humanitarianism that cared for the sick sprouted, respect for wisdom grew, and true prophets and teachers pointed the way again and again. Fear was only the scaffolding for the God concept, and evolution takes down scaffolding that has served its purpose. At the end of that road, religion comes to realize, without intermediaries, the all-powerful love of the Universal Father.
